extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in introductory proofs / discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for translating English mathematics into symbolic logic (propositional connectives, quantifiers, negation, inference) and for basic counting techniques (lists, multiplication principle, repetition constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive law
rubrics_metrics.description: P > Q = (~Q) > (~P) (Contrapositive law (2.1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This logical equivalence can be verified with truth tables and is a standard tool for transforming conditional statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: DeMorgan's laws for negating ∧ and ∨
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these rules to negate complex statements involving 'and' or 'or'; several examples show their application when forming negations of English sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commutative laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical connectives ∧ and ∨ satisfy commutativity (e.g., P ∧ Q = Q ∧ P; similarly for ∨) (2.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commutativity lets you reorder conjuncts/disjuncts without changing meaning; verify non-obvious equivalences with truth tables if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributive laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributive laws such as P ∧ (Q ∨ R) = (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R) (2.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The structure parallels algebraic distribution (e.g., p(q+r)=pq+pr); use to rewrite expressions into equivalent forms. Parentheses matter when mixing operators—see separate criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associative laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Associative laws like P ∧ (Q ∧ R) = (P ∧ Q) ∧ R and similarly for ∨ (2.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of associativity you may drop parentheses in chains of the same connective (write P ∧ Q ∧ R), but do not drop parentheses when different connectives are mixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses essential when mixing ∧ and ∨
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is a mix of ∧ and ∨, parentheses are essential; e.g., P ∨ (Q ∧ R) and (P ∨ Q) ∧ R are not logically equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not remove parentheses in mixed expressions; the exercises emphasize verifying non-equivalence with truth tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use truth tables to verify equivalences
rubrics_metrics.description: Those equivalences that are not immediately obvious can be verified with truth tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly suggests constructing truth tables to check logical equivalences and inference rules; this is a standard method for validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and use of quantifiers (∀ and ∃)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce ∀ (for all) and ∃ (there exists). For example, 'Every element of X is odd' is written ∀x ∈ X, P(x); 'There exists an element of X that is odd' is ∃x ∈ X, P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantifiers succinctly replace infinite conjunctions/disjunctions; the symbol ∀ is the universal quantifier and ∃ is the existential quantifier. Use them to form quantified statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth conditions for quantified statements
rubrics_metrics.description: A universally quantified statement ∀x∈X, P(x) is true iff P(x) is true for every x∈X. An existentially quantified statement ∃x∈X, P(x) is true iff there is at least one x∈X with P(x) true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives examples of true and false quantified statements to illustrate these conditions; use them when evaluating quantified assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of quantifiers matters
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statement contains two quantifiers you must be very alert to their order, for reversing the order can change the meaning (Example 2.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate that ∀x ∃y … is not equivalent to ∃y ∀x …. Always check the order when translating or negating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid casual language mistakes about quantification
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful in mathematical context: 'All students do not pay full tuition' is ambiguous/wrong; use 'Not all students pay full tuition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical writing demands precise quantifier usage; common English phrasing can invert meaning and must be corrected when formalizing statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied universal quantifier for unquantified conditionals
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics, whenever P(x) and Q(x) are open sentences about elements x in some set X, an expression of form P(x) > Q(x) is understood to be the statement ∀x ∈ X, P(x) > Q(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors often omit the ∀ when writing conditional statements about variables; remember the implied universal quantifier when interpreting or proving such statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / truth condition of a conditional
rubrics_metrics.description: If P and Q are statements or open sentences, then 'If P, then Q' is a statement. This statement is true if it’s impossible for P to be true while Q is false; it is false if there is at least one instance in which P is true but Q is false (Definition 2.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition aligns with the truth table for →; use it when assessing conditional claims and when negating conditionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translating English to symbolic logic — attend to meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating, be attentive to intended meaning. Don’t automatically replace every 'and' with ∧ and 'or' with ∨. For example, 'At least one of the integers x and y is even' should be (x is even) ∨ (y is even), not (x is even) ∧ (y is even). The logical meaning of 'but' is captured by 'and.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parse English sentences carefully; use the examples provided to guide correct symbolization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation rules for quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: ~(∀x∈X, P(x)) = ∃x∈X, ~P(x) and ~(∃x∈X, P(x)) = ∀x∈X, ~P(x) (Equations (2.8) and (2.9)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These equivalences conform to everyday language but pin down precise mathematical meaning. Use them iteratively when negating statements with multiple quantifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation of a conditional
rubrics_metrics.description: ~(P → Q) = P ∧ ~Q (Equation (2.10)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since P→Q is false exactly when P is true and Q false, use this form when negating conditionals (including quantified conditionals after applying quantifier-negation rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negating complex statements — use DeMorgan and quantifier rules
rubrics_metrics.description: To negate complex statements, apply DeMorgan's laws for ∧/∨ and the quantifier negation rules; multiple quantifiers require several iterations of the quantifier-negation rules (Example 2.13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work step-by-step, shifting negation inward while swapping connectives and quantifiers as required; examples illustrate the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of inference to derive conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Common inference patterns include modus ponens (from P→Q and P infer Q), modus tollens (from P→Q and ~Q infer ~P), elimination patterns, conjunction introduction/elimination, and disjunction introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents the patterns in sequent form and emphasizes internalizing these rules as they are used constantly in proofs; truth tables justify their validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and importance of logic in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic provides exact meanings for connectives via truth tables, rules of inference produce new statements from known ones, and equivalence rules (e.g., DeMorgan) help rewrite statements into useful forms. Logic underlies mathematical writing and reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although symbolic notation may be used less frequently beyond this chapter, the ideas are applied mentally when parsing proofs; maintain a firm grasp for clear mathematical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and properties of lists
rubrics_metrics.description: A list is an ordered sequence of objects, denoted (a,b,c,…). Lists differ from sets since order matters and repetition is allowed; the empty list () has length zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equal lists must have exactly the same entries in the same positions. The chapter uses lists/strings to model processes (coin tosses, rolls, phone numbers, bytes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication Principle (Fact 3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose in making a list of length n there are a1 choices for the first entry, a2 choices for the second, …, an choices for the nth. Then the total number of different lists is the product a1·a2·…·an.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tree-diagram intuition is given; you need not draw the tree—just multiply the numbers. Examples include license plates and café order choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish repetition allowed vs. not allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two types of list-counting problems: repetition allowed (entries may repeat) and repetition not allowed (non-repetitive lists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When repetition is allowed, each slot has the same number of choices; when not allowed, available choices decrease as you fill slots (e.g., n·(n−1)·(n−2)… ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double-counting; use complementary counting or careful partitioning
rubrics_metrics.description: When counting 'lists that contain at least one E' naive partitioning by position can overcount because lists with multiple E's belong to multiple categories (example shows overcounting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use complementary counting (total minus lists with no E) or ensure disjoint partitioning to avoid double-counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: When constraints depend on earlier choices, order filling matters
rubrics_metrics.description: In non-repetitive lists with positional restrictions (e.g., first entry must be B/C/D and last must be a vowel), naive application of the multiplication principle may fail because the number of choices for later positions depends on earlier choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fill the restricted positions first (or otherwise handle dependencies) and then apply the multiplication principle to the remaining slots, as illustrated in Example 3.4.
